title: Funds and fees
blurb: Stocks, mutual funds and ETFs, and what a yearly fee does over time.

levels.title: Three ways to own
learn: Tell a stock, a mutual fund and an ETF apart.
Say what a fund holds and who chooses it.

cards.text: You can own a piece of the market in three ways. You can buy one company's stock. You can buy a mutual fund. Or you can buy an ETF. A stock is a share of one company. This level shows how the three differ.
A fund is a basket. One purchase holds many companies at once. Omar puts $1,200 into a fund that holds 60 companies in equal parts. In this simple picture, $20.00 of his money goes to each company.

A mutual fund and an ETF both hold a basket. The difference is how they trade. A mutual fund has one price a day. An ETF trades like a stock: its price changes all day while the market is open. A stock also changes all day.

Someone decides what goes in a fund: a manager who picks, or a rule. An index is a list, such as the 60 biggest companies in a country. An index fund follows the list and makes no picks, so it usually costs less.
Here are the three side by side. A fund charges a yearly fee, and the next levels show what it does to your money. A stock has no fund fee.
In the game's Exchange, prices move once a world month. Its funds have a ticker and a buy price and a sell price, like a stock, so they work like ETFs. Look at them on the Exchange.

levels.title: Kinds of funds
learn: Name five common kinds of fund by what they hold.
Match the Exchange's funds to their kinds.

cards.text: Funds differ in what is in the basket. Five common kinds are money market, bond, index, actively managed and balanced. To tell them apart, ask one question: what does the fund hold?
Here are the five kinds and what each holds. A bond is a loan to a government or a company. A treasury bill is a short loan to a government. A stock fund can follow a list or have a manager pick.

figure.title: Five kinds of fund
rows: Short-term loans, such as treasury bills
The companies on a list, in the list's weights
Stocks a manager picks to try to beat the market
A mix of stocks and bonds, such as 60% and 40%

cards.text: A money market fund holds treasury bills and other short-term loans, and it aims to keep your money steady. It counts as a cash equivalent. A bond fund holds government and company bonds. Both hold loans, not shares of companies.

An index fund holds the companies on a list in the same weights as the list, and picks nothing. An actively managed fund has a manager who chooses, say, 30 stocks the manager expects to beat the market. Such funds usually charge more.

A balanced fund holds stocks and bonds in a set mix, such as 60% stocks and 40% bonds. When stocks rise, the stock part grows past 60%. Rebalancing moves money back to the set mix. A balanced fund does this for you.
The Exchange has three funds. DAAX holds every company in town. DAAB holds bonds. DAAG is 60% DAAX and 40% DAAB, rebalanced every month, so it is a balanced fund. It has no money market fund.

levels.title: The yearly fee
learn: Say what a fund's MER is and how it is paid.
Work out the fee in dollars and the return you keep.

cards.text: A fund charges a yearly fee called the MER, the management expense ratio. It is a percent of what you hold in the fund. It is taken out of the fund's return before you see the return, so no bill ever arrives.
Say you hold $10,000 in Fund C, which charges 2.25% a year. The fee for the year is 2.25% of $10,000, which is $225.00. You do not write a cheque. Your fund simply earns less.

So you can count the fee as coming off the return. Say the market earns 6% in a year and Fund C charges 2.25%. You keep 6% - 2.25% = 3.75%. Real funds take the fee a little at a time, so this is a close, simple way to count it.
Funds A, B and C are made-up funds for this unit. Here is what each one lets you keep when the market earns 6% in a year. The bigger the fee, the less you keep.

A fund's own page lists its MER. Use the fund company's page, not a news article, since articles quote old numbers. A past return only shows how one period went, and it does not promise the next. You cannot know a future return, but you can read what a fund charges.
The Exchange puts a Fund fee (MER) line on each fund's card. The game starts with 0.06% a year for DAAX, 0.10% for DAAB and 0.20% for DAAG. The fee comes off the price a little each month.

levels.title: What a fee takes over time
learn: Work out how a fee grows into a big gap, year by year.
See how a fee slows doubling.

cards.text: The class example: $10,000 is invested once and left for 30 years. The market earns 6% a year. Fund C charges 2.25%, so it keeps 3.75%, and each year the balance is multiplied by 1.0375. Year 1: $10,375.00. Year 2: $10,764.06.
Each year, the money grows on last year's balance. Here are both balances every five years, rounded to the dollar. Both grow, but Fund C grows slower, and the gap widens.
Funds A and B charge 0.25% and 1.00%. At year 30, no fee gives $57,435, Fund A $53,507, Fund B $43,219 and Fund C $30,175. Fund C ends $27,260 below no fee, which is 47.5% less.

The longer you hold, the more a fee takes. After 10 years, Fund C has $14,450 against $17,908 with no fee: 19.3% less. After 30 years it is 47.5% less. The fee is paid every year, and the money it takes stops growing too.

The fee does not shrink when returns do. If the market earns only 3%, Fund C still charges 2.25% and you keep 0.75%. The fee takes 75% of that year's return, not 37.5%. Over 30 years $10,000 ends at $12,513, against $24,273 with no fee.

A fee also slows doubling. The Rule of 72 estimates it: divide 72 by the yearly percent to get the years. At 6% that is 72 / 6 = 12 years. A 2% fee leaves 4%, and 72 / 4 = 18 years. The fee takes a third of the return but adds six years of waiting.
